blueprint_topic: Management of Care — advance care planning, goals-of-care communication, client advocacy, and future treatment preferences in serious respiratory illness
stem: A nurse participates in advance care planning with a client who has COPD and is at risk for future severe exacerbations. Which outcome best reflects the purpose of this discussion?

options.A: Clarify and document the client's values and preferences for future care, including ventilation choices, before acute illness limits participation.
options.B: Choose a health care proxy now, but defer discussion of treatment preferences until a future exacerbation requires an ICU-level decision.
options.C: Document a standing preference for mechanical ventilation so clinicians can avoid revisiting goals as the client's respiratory illness changes.
options.D: Reserve the discussion for a point when disease-directed treatment has been exhausted, because advance planning is primarily an end-of-life intervention.

rationale: A is correct. Current ATS guidance for COPD exacerbations advises discussing advance care planning with patients at risk for future severe exacerbations, including treatment wishes if they become too sick to speak for themselves and whether they would want mechanical ventilation. An official ATS-led multisociety policy statement defines advance care planning as an iterative, longitudinal process that begins early in serious respiratory illness and helps patients understand and share values, goals, and preferences for future medical care; goals-of-care discussions may include specific interventions such as intubation and mechanical ventilation. B is incomplete because identifying a proxy can be part of advance planning, but treatment preferences should not be intentionally deferred until an ICU crisis. C is incorrect because advance care planning is iterative and should evolve as health status, goals, and preferences change rather than locking in one intervention and avoiding future review. D is incorrect because advance care planning and palliative approaches can occur alongside disease-directed treatment and are not reserved for the point when treatment options are exhausted.
educational_objective: Use advance care planning to clarify and document a client's evolving values, goals, and preferences for future treatment before acute respiratory deterioration may limit decision-making participation.
source_organization: American Thoracic Society (ATS); American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine (AAHPM); Hospice and Palliative Nurses Association (HPNA); Social Work Hospice and Palliative Care Network (SWHPN); National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Exacerbation of COPD; Palliative Care Early in the Care Continuum among Patients with Serious Respiratory Illness: An Official ATS/AAHPM/HPNA/SWHPN Policy Statement; Palliative Care for People with Respiratory Disease or Critical Illness; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan
source_version_date: ATS Exacerbation of COPD online version updated March 2024 and rechecked 2026-08-20; ATS-led policy statement published 2022 and current on ATS/Oxford/PMC when rechecked 2026-08-20; 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan effective April 2026
source_locator: ATS 'Exacerbation of COPD' lines 198-202 and update line 244: patients at risk for future exacerbations may discuss advance care planning; discuss treatment wishes if too sick to speak for themselves; mechanical ventilation is given as a specific example; online version updated March 2024. Official ATS/AAHPM/HPNA/SWHPN policy statement, Advance Care Planning and Goals of Care section: ACP supports understanding/sharing values, life goals, and preferences for future medical care; discussions may include intubation and mechanical ventilation; Recommendation 3 states ACP should be an iterative longitudinal process beginning at diagnosis of serious respiratory illness and evolving with changes in health status, goals, and preferences. ATS palliative-care patient resource states palliative care can help explore values/goals/preferences and document them in advance directives. NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan Management of Care supports client rights, advance directives, advocacy, communication, and coordination of care preferences.
source_claim_supported: Current ATS and ATS-led multisociety sources directly support proactive, noncoercive, iterative advance care planning in serious respiratory illness, including clarification of future treatment preferences and mechanical-ventilation choices before loss of communication capacity. NCSBN supports the nursing advocacy and advance-directive construct.
blueprint_locator: Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care: protect client rights and autonomy, integrate advance directives into care, advocate for client preferences, communicate with the interdisciplinary team, and coordinate continuity of care.
pdf_visual_verification: NCSBN 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan evidence was visually verified earlier in this cleanup session. ATS evidence used for Q1925 is current HTML/full-text webpage content; no new PDF evidence is used.
correction_summary: Original Q1925 had a conspicuously long correct answer (154 characters versus 85-102) and distractors that were easy to eliminate. The item was rebuilt around the broader ATS definition of advance care planning: proactive, iterative clarification of values and future treatment preferences, including ventilation decisions, rather than forced refusal, crisis-only discussion, or end-of-life-only planning. All four alternatives are realistic planning strategies with balanced lengths. Independent post-fetch reread found no unresolved source, clinical, autonomy, timing, ambiguity, cueing, blueprint, or second-answer conflict.

option_audit.A: Correct; directly reflects proactive clarification/documentation of future treatment preferences before acute deterioration limits participation.
option_audit.B: Plausible proxy-focused partial plan; incorrect because proxy designation can be useful but does not justify deferring treatment-preference discussion until an ICU crisis.
option_audit.C: Plausible documentation shortcut; incorrect because ACP is iterative and should be revisited as health status and goals change.
option_audit.D: Plausible end-of-life misconception; incorrect because ACP and palliative approaches can be integrated alongside disease-directed care earlier in serious illness.

cueing_audit.absolute_words: No option relies on only/all/always/never/must-type absolute wording.
cueing_audit.answer_length: Final option lengths: A 147, B 137, C 143, D 153 characters; the correct answer is not the longest and choices are tightly balanced.
cueing_audit.grammatical_lexical: All four options describe plausible advance-planning strategies and differ in timing, scope, or revisability rather than obvious wording quality.
cueing_audit.second_answer_risk: Independent adversarial reread found no defensible second answer. B includes a valid proxy concept but improperly defers goals discussion; C contradicts the iterative nature of ACP; D wrongly restricts ACP to exhausted disease-directed treatment. A is uniquely best.

independent_second_pass: PASS — post-fetch adversarial reread independently rechecked stem, A/B/C/D, correct key, rationale, objective, ATS COPD guidance, the ATS-led multisociety ACP policy statement, mechanical-ventilation framing, iterative/longitudinal timing, coexistence with disease-directed care, NCSBN Management of Care fit, cueing and second-answer risk. The item does not coerce refusal of life-sustaining treatment and does not treat ACP as a one-time or end-of-life-only event. No unresolved conflict identified.
